title: LLMs as Writing Assistants: Exploring Perspectives on Sense of Ownership and Reasoning
venue: The Third Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants (In2Writing '24)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how people perceive ownership and authorship when using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT as writing assistants. The authors focus on two related questions: whether sense of ownership differs by content type, especially creative versus non-creative writing, and how people reconcile claiming authorship of AI-assisted text while not fully feeling that they own it. The study is motivated by the growing use of LLMs in writing and the psychological tension created when humans contribute prompts or edits but the text itself is machine-generated.

The approach is a brief survey study of 35 participants. Respondents were asked about their perceived contribution to non-creative writing (such as assignments) and creative writing (such as stories or poems), whether they would submit LLM-generated content under their own name, whether they felt they owned content produced by ChatGPT, and whether that sense of ownership changed when they were reminded of their prompting or editing role. The paper does not evaluate learning outcomes or writing performance directly; instead, it examines self-reported perceptions about contribution, ownership, and authorship.

The population consisted predominantly of university students aged 18-24, with most participants from science backgrounds and reporting relatively high technology awareness. The paper situates the study in the context of LLM-assisted writing, likely in higher-education-related use cases such as assignments, though it is not framed as a classroom intervention. The authors are based in Bangladesh, and the participant description suggests a university-student sample from that context.

The main conclusions are that participants reported stronger ownership and contribution in non-creative writing than in creative writing, where they tended to credit the LLM more heavily. The study also found a mismatch between authorship and ownership: many participants were willing to submit AI-generated text under their own name even when they did not fully claim ownership of it. Reminding participants about their role in prompting and especially editing increased perceived ownership, suggesting that active human involvement shapes how ownership and authorship are experienced in AI-assisted writing.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI large language model chatbot used for generating and assisting with written text.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a writing assistant in a short survey examining users' perceptions of contribution, ownership, and authorship in non-creative and creative writing tasks.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of 35 participants, respondents reported stronger perceived contribution/ownership in non-creative writing (e.g., STEM assignments, formal letters) and lower perceived contribution in creative writing (e.g., poems, stories, birthday wishes). The paper describes distributional differences qualitatively and via figures, but does not report effect sizes or inferential statistics.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived contribution/ownership in ChatGPT-assisted non-creative versus creative writing tasks

findings.finding_summary: Participants were often willing to self-declare authorship of ChatGPT-generated text while not claiming ownership of it: ownership responses were No 51.5%, Maybe 31.4%, while willingness to submit LLM-generated content under their own name was Yes 28.6%, Maybe 48.6%. This indicates a mismatch between perceived ownership and authorship in ChatGPT-assisted writing.
findings.measure: Self-reported ownership of ChatGPT-generated content and willingness to claim authorship

findings.finding_summary: Reminding participants of their role in prompting ChatGPT increased claimed ownership of the generated content: Yes increased from 17.1% to 28.6%, Maybe increased from 31.4% to 48.6%, and No decreased from 51.4% to 22.9%. The paper interprets this as evidence that highlighting user contribution raises perceived ownership.
findings.measure: Change in self-reported ownership after reminder about prompt contribution

findings.finding_summary: After participants were reminded that they had modified ChatGPT's original response, 62.9% claimed ownership of the content. The study concludes that active editing/refinement of AI-generated text increases perceived ownership/authorship.
findings.measure: Self-reported ownership after editing/modifying ChatGPT-generated text

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small survey study (n=35) with self-reported perceptions and no experimental learning outcome design, effect sizes, or causal identification. The evidence is empirical but limited and primarily descriptive.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports shifts in perceptions of ownership/authorship, but impacts are based on descriptive survey percentages rather than validated educational outcome gains or effect sizes. Overall impact is suggestive but unclear.
